topics.h: Your morning cup of chai needs a tea farmer in Assam, a truck driver, a shopkeeper and a price you can afford. Who studies how all these people and places are linked? Social scientists do!
p: Social science is the careful, systematic study of human society: how people live together, work, make rules, use resources and change over time.
In Classes 9 and 10 it is studied through four main disciplines: History, Geography, Political Science and Economics.
History studies the human past and how things changed; Geography studies places, location and how people and the environment affect each other.
Political Science studies governance, institutions, power and how public decisions are made; Economics studies how people make choices about limited resources.
Social science depends on evidence. A good social scientist separates personal opinion from claims that can be supported by facts.

ex.q: Think it through: A new bus route starts in your town. Which question would each social science discipline ask about it?
st: Geography: Which places and villages does the route connect, and why was this road chosen?
Economics: How much does a ticket cost, and who can now reach jobs or markets more cheaply?
Political Science: Who decided to start the route, and how did the local government make the decision?
History: How did people of this town travel twenty or fifty years ago, and what has changed?
ex.a: Each discipline looks at the same event from a different angle: place, money and choices, decision-making, and change over time.

topics.rl: When you read a newspaper story about floods, elections, prices of onions or an old fort being restored, you are reading social science in action.

topics.t: How we know about the past: sources and evidence
topics.h: A coin found in a farmer's field in Andhra Pradesh can tell us which king ruled, what language was used and how far traders travelled. Clues like this are a historian's treasure.
p: Historians use sources: things from the past that give evidence about it.
Archaeological sources are material remains such as tools, pottery, beads, buildings, terracotta figurines and fossils, found by careful excavation.
Epigraphic sources are inscriptions carved or written on hard surfaces such as rock, pillars or copper plates; numismatic sources are coins.
Written (literary) sources include texts such as the Arthashastra, credited to Kautilya; oral traditions, songs and family records (genealogies) also preserve memory of the past.
Every source must be checked. Historians compare sources and ask who made them and why. Scientific methods such as carbon-14 dating help find the age of ancient remains.

ex.q: Think it through: An old copper plate records a king giving land to a village temple. What can a historian learn from it, and what should she be careful about?
st: It is an epigraphic source, because the record is engraved on metal.
It can show the king's name, the language and script used, place names and how land was granted.
It was written on the king's orders, so it may praise the king more than ordinary people would.
She should compare it with other sources such as coins, other inscriptions and excavated remains.
ex.a: It gives useful evidence about rulers, language and land grants, but it must be checked against other sources because it shows the ruler's point of view.

topics.rl: Museums such as the National Museum in New Delhi display coins, seals, pottery and inscriptions, and each label tells you what kind of source it is.

topics.t: How history, geography, civics and economics connect
topics.h: When the monsoon fails in a village in Marathwada, crops dry up, families lose income, the government plans relief and some people migrate. One drought, four subjects!
p: Real problems rarely fit into a single subject. Studying them using several disciplines together is called an interdisciplinary approach.
Geography gives the spatial perspective: where something happens and why that location matters, using maps, globes, atlases and GIS.
Economics shows effects on incomes, prices and jobs; Political Science shows how governments and local bodies such as panchayats respond.
History shows how a place or problem has changed over time, for example how settlements grew after farming and the taming of animals began.

Ideas from India's past, such as vasudhaiva kutumbakam ('the world is one family'), remind us that societies everywhere are connected. Sustainable development means meeting today's needs without harming the ability of future generations to meet theirs.

ex.q: Think it through: India has a long coastline. How can this one geographical fact connect to history and economics?
st: Geography: a long coastline gives many natural harbours and access to the sea.
History: for thousands of years ships from Indian ports traded with distant lands, carrying goods and ideas.
Economics: ports create jobs in fishing, shipping and trade, and goods can be exchanged with other countries.
So a fact about location helps explain past events and present livelihoods.
ex.a: The coastline (geography) made sea trade possible in the past (history) and supports jobs and trade today (economics).

topics.rl: Planning a new metro line in a city needs maps (geography), budgets (economics), government approval (political science) and knowledge of old buildings in the way (history).

topics.ch: Early Humans and Beginning of Civilisation
topics.t: Early humans: from hunter-gatherers to the first artists
topics.h: Thousands of years ago, someone in a rock shelter in Madhya Pradesh dipped a finger in red colour and painted a running animal. Those paintings at Bhimbetka still survive!
p: Humans evolved over a very long time. Several human species once existed, such as Homo erectus and the Neanderthals, but Homo sapiens (modern humans) is the only human species living today.
Homo erectus made handaxes and cleavers and was among the early humans to spread out of Africa into Asia and Europe. Over time, skulls became larger and rounder and jaws and teeth became smaller.
Palaeolithic (Old Stone Age) people were hunter-gatherers: they hunted animals, gathered wild plants, moved in search of food and water, and lived in caves, rock shelters or temporary camps.
In the Mesolithic (Middle Stone Age), people used microliths: tiny stone tools often fitted into wooden or bone handles to make arrows, spears and sickles.

Before writing, people communicated through speech, gestures, body decoration, engravings and paintings. The rock shelters of Bhimbetka in Madhya Pradesh, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, preserve such early art.

ex.q: Think it through: Archaeologists find a cave with ash, animal bones and many small stone blades. What can they infer about the people who lived there?
st: Ash suggests the people used fire, for warmth, light, cooking or keeping animals away.
Animal bones suggest they hunted animals for food.
Small stone blades (microliths) suggest they made fine tools, probably fixed into handles.
Since there are no farm tools or houses, they were probably hunter-gatherers who used the cave as a shelter.
ex.a: They were probably Stone Age hunter-gatherers who used fire, hunted animals and made microlith tools.

topics.rl: When you visit a museum and see a stone handaxe behind glass, remember that someone shaped it carefully by striking one stone with another.

topics.ch: Early Humans and Beginning of Civilisation
topics.t: The Neolithic revolution: farming and settled life
topics.h: Imagine never having to chase your dinner again! When people learned to grow wheat and barley and keep goats, life changed forever.
p: The Neolithic (New Stone Age) brought a great change called the Neolithic revolution: people began growing crops and taming (domesticating) animals such as cattle, sheep and goats.
Farming meant people stayed near their fields, so they built permanent houses and villages. They used polished stone tools, made pottery to store grain and began weaving cloth.
Mehrgarh, in present-day Balochistan (Pakistan), is one of the earliest farming villages in South Asia. People there grew wheat and barley, kept animals and built mud-brick houses and storage rooms.

Extra food (surplus) could be stored, so some people could become potters, weavers or other specialists. Settled life also brought new problems such as crop failure and the need to protect stored grain.
In the Chalcolithic (Copper-Stone) age, people used copper along with stone. Later, people learned to make bronze, a mixture of copper and tin, which gave the Bronze Age its name.

ex.q: Think it through: Why did farming lead people to make pottery?
st: Farmers harvested more grain than they could eat at once.
The surplus had to be stored safely away from damp, insects and rats.
Clay pots could store grain, water and oil, and could also be used for cooking.
Since people now stayed in one place, heavy pots were not a burden to carry around.
ex.a: Settled farmers needed containers to store and cook their surplus food, so pottery became important.

topics.rl: The earthen matka that keeps water cool in many Indian homes in summer is part of a pottery tradition that began with the first farmers.

topics.ch: Early Humans and Beginning of Civilisation
topics.h: More than 4,000 years ago, cities in north-western India had straight streets, covered drains and standard weights. Town planners today still admire them!
p: The Harappan civilisation, also called the Indus or Sindhu-Sarasvati civilisation, was a Bronze Age civilisation. Its mature, urban phase is dated to about 2600-1900 BCE.
Important sites include Harappa and Mohenjo-daro (now in Pakistan), and Dholavira and Lothal (Gujarat), Kalibangan (Rajasthan) and Rakhigarhi (Haryana) in India.

Cities were planned with streets meeting at right angles, houses of baked bricks of standard proportions and covered drains. Mohenjo-daro had the Great Bath, Dholavira had large water reservoirs and Lothal had a dockyard.

Harappans used standard cubical stone weights. Smaller weights followed a doubling pattern (1, 2, 4, 8, 16...) and larger ones used multiples of ten. Kalibangan shows a ploughed field with criss-cross furrows.
They traded with Mesopotamia, whose records probably called the region 'Meluhha'. The Harappan script, found on seals and pots, has not yet been deciphered.

ex.q: Think it through: Why have scholars still not been able to read the Harappan script?
st: Most inscriptions are very short, often only a few signs on a seal.
No bilingual inscription has been found, like the Rosetta Stone that gave the same text in known and unknown scripts.
We do not know for certain which language the Harappans spoke.
Without longer texts or a key, scholars cannot confidently match signs to sounds or words.
ex.a: The inscriptions are short and there is no bilingual 'key', so the script remains undeciphered.

topics.rl: Dholavira in the Rann of Kutch became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2021, and visitors can still see its stone reservoirs built to save rainwater.

topics.ch: Early Humans and Beginning of Civilisation
topics.t: Egypt, Mesopotamia and China: river civilisations
topics.h: Why did so many early civilisations grow beside great rivers? Think of the Nile, the Tigris and Euphrates, and the Huang He: water, fertile soil and boats!
p: Egypt grew along the Nile. Its yearly floods left fertile mud for farming. Rulers called pharaohs were very powerful; huge pyramids, such as the Great Pyramid of Giza, were built as royal tombs.

Egyptians believed in life after death and preserved bodies by mummification. They wrote in hieroglyphics on papyrus; the Rosetta Stone, carrying the same text in hieroglyphic, Demotic and Greek, helped scholars decipher it.

Mesopotamia means 'the land between the rivers' (the Tigris and the Euphrates, in present-day Iraq). Sumerians lived in city-states, built stepped temples called ziggurats and wrote in cuneiform, wedge-shaped marks pressed into clay.
King Hammurabi of Babylon issued a famous code of laws; punishments often depended on a person's social status. The Epic of Gilgamesh is one of the world's oldest stories.

Chinese civilisation grew along the Huang He (Yellow River). Shang rulers used oracle bones, heating bones or shells and reading the cracks, to seek answers about the future. Chinese writing is logographic and the Chinese learned to make silk.

ex.q: Think it through: What did the Harappan, Egyptian, Mesopotamian and Chinese civilisations have in common?
st: All grew in river valleys with water and fertile soil for farming.
Farm surplus supported cities, specialised crafts and trade.
Each developed a form of writing: Harappan script, hieroglyphics, cuneiform and Chinese characters.
Each had organised government and used bronze.
ex.a: River valleys, farming surplus, cities, crafts, trade, writing, organised government and bronze technology.

topics.rl: Rivers still shape where people live: think of how many Indian cities, such as Varanasi, Patna and Kolkata, stand on the banks of the Ganga or its branches.

topics.ch: State and Society up to 1000 CE
topics.t: From jana to janapada to mahajanapada
topics.h: How did small groups of families, herding cattle and singing hymns, grow into big kingdoms with capitals, armies and taxes? Let us follow the journey along the Ganga plains.
p: Early society was organised in kulas (families or clans) and janas (larger kin-based groups, often called tribes). A jana was led by a raja; the Bharatas were one of the janas mentioned in the Rig Veda.
The raja did not rule alone. Vedic assemblies such as the sabha, the samiti and the vidatha discussed matters and could check the raja's power.

Over time, people of a jana settled in a region, which came to be called a janapada (the land where a jana set foot). Some janapadas grew into larger, powerful states called mahajanapadas. Buddhist and Jaina texts list sixteen mahajanapadas.

Iron tools helped clear forests and plough more land, more crops such as paddy were grown and settlements multiplied in the Ganga plains. Pottery styles of this time include Painted Grey Ware and the glossy Northern Black Polished Ware.

Magadha, in present-day Bihar, became the most powerful mahajanapada. It had fertile land, rivers for transport, iron ore and forests with elephants. Its capitals were Rajagriha (Rajgir) and later Pataliputra (Patna).

ex.q: Think it through: Why did Magadha grow stronger than the other mahajanapadas?
st: The Ganga and Son rivers gave water, fertile soil and easy transport.
Good harvests meant the rulers could collect more taxes.
Nearby iron ore gave tools and weapons; forests supplied elephants for the army.
Capable rulers used these advantages to expand their territory.
ex.a: Fertile land, rivers, iron ore, elephants and ambitious rulers together made Magadha the strongest mahajanapada.

topics.rl: Rajgir and Patna in Bihar still carry the history of Rajagriha and Pataliputra, and the name 'Bharat' for our country has very old roots.

topics.ch: State and Society up to 1000 CE
topics.t: Early states and kingdoms: Mauryas to Cholas
topics.h: One rock near Girnar in Gujarat carries messages from three different rulers across hundreds of years. Rocks can be history's notice boards!
p: Chandragupta Maurya, guided by Chanakya (Kautilya), defeated the Nanda ruler Dhana Nanda and founded the Mauryan Empire in about 321 BCE, with its capital at Pataliputra.

Ashoka, the most famous Mauryan ruler, was deeply moved by the suffering of the Kalinga war (in present-day Odisha). He then followed Dhamma, a code of compassion, non-violence, tolerance and respect, spread through edicts written mostly in Prakrit in the Brahmi script.
The Junagadh rock inscription near Girnar has records of Ashoka, the Shaka ruler Rudradaman I and the Gupta ruler Skandagupta. It tells how the Sudarshana lake, built in Mauryan times, was repaired.

The Satavahanas ruled the Deccan, while the Cholas, Cheras and Pandyas ruled the far south. The Guptas built a large kingdom in the north; Samudragupta's achievements are praised in the Prayaga inscription composed by his court poet Harishena.

Later powers included the Pallavas of Kanchipuram, the Chalukyas of Badami and the Rashtrakutas. The Palas, Gurjara-Pratiharas and Rashtrakutas fought a long 'tripartite struggle' for control of Kannauj.

ex.q: Think it through: Why is the Junagadh rock inscription so valuable to historians?
st: It carries inscriptions of three rulers from different dynasties: Mauryan, Shaka and Gupta.
So one place shows how power in the region changed over centuries.
It records the repair of the Sudarshana lake, showing that rulers cared about water for farming.
Since the records are carved in stone, they survived for a very long time.
ex.a: It shows changing rulers over centuries in one place and records how a large water reservoir was built and repaired.

topics.rl: India's national emblem is adapted from the Lion Capital of Ashoka found at Sarnath, and the Ashoka Chakra appears on our national flag.

topics.ch: State and Society up to 1000 CE
topics.t: Ruling a kingdom: ideas of unity and administration
topics.h: Without phones or trains, how could a king rule lands stretching hundreds of kilometres? Smart ideas, trusted officials and village assemblies!
p: Ancient Indian texts describe dharma, a shared idea of duty, justice and right conduct, which rulers were expected to follow. Texts such as the Mahabharata and Kautilya's Arthashastra discuss the duties of kings.

The ideal of the chakravarti samrat described a ruler whose authority spread across much of the land. Great rituals such as the rajasuya and the ashvamedha were performed to show a ruler's power; names like Bharatavarsha and Jambudvipa expressed the idea of a shared land.
Kings were helped by a council of ministers (mantris) and officials such as the purohita (royal priest), the senapati (army chief) and the samaharta (in charge of collecting revenue).
Kingdoms were divided into provinces, districts and villages. A village headman (gramika) looked after the village, and local bankers, merchants and artisans were sometimes consulted.

Village assemblies managed local matters. Inscriptions at Uthiramerur (Tamil Nadu) from the Chola period describe kudavolai: names written on palm leaves were put in a pot (kudam) and drawn to choose members of village committees.

ex.q: Think it through: How is the kudavolai system similar to and different from elections today?
st: Similar: members of local committees were chosen by a fixed public procedure, not just by the king's order.
Similar: rules described who could be chosen, such as owning land and having good conduct.
Different: names were drawn by lot from a pot, while today voters cast votes for candidates.
Different: today every adult citizen can vote, which is universal adult franchise.
ex.a: Both used rules for choosing local representatives, but kudavolai drew names by lot while modern elections use votes by all adult citizens.

topics.rl: Today India has states, districts and villages or urban local bodies, and gram panchayats look after local matters, a little like the old village assemblies.

topics.ch: State and Society up to 1000 CE
topics.t: Society and economy: varna, jati, guilds and learning
topics.h: Two thousand years ago, a man donated money to weavers' guilds near Nashik so that the interest would pay for monks' robes. Guilds were like ancient banks!
p: Society was described in terms of four varnas: Brahmanas, Kshatriyas, Vaishyas and Shudras. Early Vedic texts suggest occupations were flexible: one hymn describes a family with a poet, a physician and a woman who grinds corn.

Over time varna became hereditary, and society also formed many smaller groups called jatis, often linked to occupation, region and marriage within the group. Learned women such as Gargi and Maitreyi are mentioned in the Upanishads.

Merchants and artisans formed guilds called shrenis. They set standards for their work, trained members and even accepted deposits and paid interest. A Nashik cave inscription records an endowment of 3,000 kahapanas deposited with weavers' guilds.

Trade routes such as the Uttarapatha (northern route) and Dakshinapatha (southern route) connected markets. Punch-marked coins were used, and rulers built water works like the Sudarshana lake to support farming.

Students learned in gurukulas, living with the teacher and offering gurudakshina at the end. Great centres of learning included Takshashila, Nalanda and Vikramashila. Tamil Sangam poems and the devotional songs of the Alvars and Nayanars are treasures of this age.

ex.q: Think it through: Ushavadata deposited 2,000 kahapanas with one weavers' guild and 1,000 kahapanas with another. What does this tell us about guilds?
st: The total deposit was 2,000 + 1,000 = 3,000 kahapanas.
The guilds kept the money and paid monthly interest, which was used for the monks living in the caves.
So guilds were trusted enough to hold large sums for a long time.
This shows they worked like banks as well as craft organisations.
ex.a: 3,000 kahapanas in all; guilds acted as financial institutions that accepted deposits and paid interest.

topics.rl: The ruins of Nalanda in Bihar are a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and a new Nalanda University now stands nearby at Rajgir, carrying forward its name.

topics.t: Medieval kingdoms: a changing political map
topics.h: Between 1000 and 1700 CE the map of India kept changing like a giant puzzle: new kingdoms rose, old ones fought back, and some empires grew very large.
p: Around 1000 CE many regional kingdoms ruled India, such as the Cholas in the south and the Chalukyas (Solankis) in Gujarat. Armies from Afghanistan and Central Asia began raiding and later conquering parts of north India.

In 1178, Naiki Devi of the Chalukya kingdom of Gujarat defeated the army of Muhammad Ghuri near Mount Abu. At Tarain, Prithviraj Chauhan defeated Ghuri in 1191, but Ghuri won the second battle of Tarain in 1192.
The Delhi Sultanate began in 1206 with Qutbuddin Aibak and lasted until 1526. Sultans gave officers revenue assignments called iqtas. Many local and regional rulers resisted its expansion.
In the south, the Vijayanagara kingdom was founded in 1336 by Harihara and Bukka. In 1526 Babur defeated Ibrahim Lodi at the first battle of Panipat and founded Mughal rule.

Akbar organised Mughal officials through the mansab system, giving each a rank. Court ceremonies such as the Nauroz festival and jharokha darshan displayed the emperor's power. Rajputs, Ahoms, Marathas, Sikhs and Jats were among those who resisted Mughal power at different times.

ex.q: Think it through: The two battles of Tarain were fought in 1191 and 1192. What do their results show about this period?
st: In 1191 Prithviraj Chauhan won, showing that the invading army could be defeated.
In 1192 Muhammad Ghuri won, which opened the way for the Delhi Sultanate in 1206.
So power changed hands quickly, and the result of a single battle could change history.
It also shows that resistance continued even when a battle was lost, as later regional rulers kept fighting.
ex.a: Power shifted back and forth: the first battle was won by Prithviraj, the second by Ghuri, leading to the Delhi Sultanate.

topics.rl: The Qutub Minar complex and Hampi are both UNESCO World Heritage Sites that you can visit today to see buildings from this period.

topics.t: Resistance in the west and north: Rajputs, Marathas and Jats
topics.h: Picture the rocky Aravalli hills of Mewar and the steep Sahyadri forts of Maharashtra. Rulers here used the land itself as a shield.
p: Rajput kingdoms such as Mewar defended their independence. Rana Sanga of Mewar fought Babur at Khanua in 1527. Akbar's army besieged Chittor in 1567-68, and some other Rajput houses chose alliances with the Mughals instead.

Maharana Pratap of Mewar refused to accept Mughal authority. He fought the Mughal army led by Raja Man Singh of Amber at Haldighati in 1576; the Afghan commander Hakim Khan Sur fought on Pratap's side. Supported by the Bhils and the hilly Aravalli terrain, he continued his struggle for many years.

Shivaji built the idea of Swarajya (self-rule) in Maharashtra. He used hill forts and sea forts, fast-moving cavalry and surprise attacks, and was crowned Chhatrapati at Raigad in 1674. A council of eight ministers, the Ashtapradhan, helped him govern.
The Jats, mostly peasants of the region around Mathura and Agra, rose against heavy Mughal revenue demands under leaders such as Gokula. Their resistance had strong economic causes.
Resistance was not only about battles: it depended on terrain, forts, local support, good organisation and the wish to protect one's own traditions.

ex.q: Think it through: Why were hill forts so useful to Shivaji?
st: Forts on steep hills were hard for large armies with heavy guns to attack.
They could store food and water, so defenders could hold out for a long time.
From the forts, small fast forces could make surprise raids and return to safety.
Sea forts like Sindhudurg also protected the coast and trade.
ex.a: The forts used the difficult terrain to protect small forces, store supplies and launch surprise attacks.

topics.rl: In 2025, twelve forts, mostly in Maharashtra and one in Tamil Nadu, were added to UNESCO's World Heritage list as the 'Maratha Military Landscapes of India'.

topics.t: Resistance in the east and south: the Ahoms and Vijayanagara
topics.h: On the mighty Brahmaputra, Ahom boats outmanoeuvred a much larger Mughal fleet. Rivers, hills and clever organisation helped the Ahoms stay independent for centuries.
p: The Ahom kingdom of Assam was founded by Sukaphaa in 1228. Ahom rulers governed the Brahmaputra valley for nearly six hundred years, until 1826.
Under the paik system, adult men (paiks) served the state by turns, as soldiers, builders or workers, in return for land. This gave the Ahoms a ready army and workforce.

Ahom commander Lachit Borphukan led the defence against the Mughals. In the battle of Saraighat (1671), fought on the Brahmaputra near Guwahati, the Ahoms defeated the Mughal fleet, using their knowledge of the river and hills.

Vijayanagara (capital near present-day Hampi, on the Tungabhadra river) became a powerful kingdom in the south. Prince Kumara Kampana led a campaign that ended the Sultanate at Madurai; his wife Gangadevi wrote about it in the Sanskrit poem Madhura Vijayam.

Krishnadevaraya was Vijayanagara's most famous ruler and a poet who wrote Amuktamalyada in Telugu. After the battle of Talikota in 1565 against an alliance of Deccan Sultanates, the capital was sacked, but Nayaka rulers carried its traditions forward in the south.

ex.q: Think it through: How did geography help the Ahoms defend themselves?
st: The Brahmaputra is wide, with strong currents and many channels, which the Ahoms knew well.
Their boats and soldiers could move quickly on the river, while outsiders struggled.
Hills and forests around the valley made it hard for a large army to advance.
Combined with the paik system, which gave them organised manpower, this helped them win at Saraighat.
ex.a: Knowledge of the river, hills and forests, together with good organisation, helped the Ahoms resist a larger army.

topics.rl: Every year on 24 November, Assam celebrates Lachit Divas to remember the courage of Lachit Borphukan.

topics.h: Resilience means bouncing back. Even in hard times, songs of devotion, festivals, temples, trade and learning kept India's traditions alive and growing.
p: Resistance means opposing a threat or an authority one does not accept; resilience means enduring hardship, adapting and recovering. Both shaped this period.

The Sikh Gurus built a strong community. Guru Arjan Dev compiled the Adi Granth; he was put to death in 1606 on the orders of Emperor Jahangir, and Sikhs remember this as his martyrdom. Guru Hargobind adopted the ideas of miri and piri (worldly and spiritual authority) and built the Akal Takht. Guru Tegh Bahadur was martyred in Delhi in 1675 on Aurangzeb's orders, and Guru Gobind Singh founded the Khalsa in 1699.

Bhakti saints spread devotion in people's own languages: Kabir (nirguna bhakti, devotion to a God without form), Tulsidas (Ramcharitmanas in Awadhi), Surdas (songs on Krishna in Braj), Mirabai, and Chaitanya Mahaprabhu, who led group singing (sankirtan) in Bengal. Sufi saints, living in khanqahs, also taught love and devotion.
Temples destroyed in wars were often rebuilt. The Kashi Vishwanath temple in Varanasi was rebuilt several times; the present temple was built by Ahilyabai Holkar of Indore in 1780.

Economic life continued: merchants used hundis (letters of credit) and sarrafs (money-changers), ports like Surat and Masulipatnam traded overseas, and communities built stepwells, tanks and canals for water.

ex.q: Think it through: How did Bhakti saints help traditions survive in difficult times?
st: They taught that devotion to God mattered more than costly rituals, so anyone could take part.
They composed songs in people's own languages, like Awadhi, Braj and Tamil, which everyone could understand.
Songs could be sung at home and in groups, even when large temples were damaged.
Their poems are still sung today, so the ideas passed down for centuries.
ex.a: By spreading devotion through simple songs in local languages that ordinary people could sing and remember.

topics.rl: Tulsidas's Ramcharitmanas is recited in many homes, Kabir's dohas are taught in school, and Rani ki Vav, a stepwell in Patan, Gujarat, appears on the ₹100 note.

qa.q: Which of these best describes social science?
qa.a: The systematic study of human society and relationships
qa.e: Social science studies people in society: how they live, work, govern themselves and use resources.

qa.q: Meera asks, 'Why is there more rainfall in Kerala than in Rajasthan?' Which discipline mainly deals with this question?
qa.e: Rainfall patterns and differences between places are studied in Geography.

qa.q: Which discipline studies how people make choices about limited resources such as money, time and land?
qa.e: Economics studies production, exchange, distribution and the choices people make because resources are limited.

qa.q: A student studies how a panchayat plans a new village well and who takes the final decision. Which discipline is this?
qa.e: Decision-making by local government bodies such as panchayats is part of Political Science.

qa.q: Which is a statement based on evidence rather than opinion?
qa.a: The census counts the population of India
qa.e: That the census counts India's population can be checked. The other statements are personal preferences.

qa.q: Why do social scientists study the same event from several angles?
qa.a: Because one angle usually gives an incomplete picture
qa.e: A flood, for example, has geographical, economic, political and historical sides. Looking at all of them gives a fuller understanding.

qa.q: Which question would a historian most likely ask about a village market?
qa.a: How has the market changed over the last hundred years?
qa.e: Historians study change over time, so they ask how the market looked and worked in the past.

qa.q: What does 'social interdependence' mean?
qa.a: People depend on one another to meet their everyday needs
qa.e: A simple meal needs farmers, transporters and sellers. People rely on each other's work.

qa.q: A silver coin with a ruler's name is found at an old site. What type of source is it?
qa.e: Coins are numismatic sources. They can show rulers, metals used, symbols and trade links.

qa.q: Words carved on a rock or stone pillar are an example of which source?
qa.e: Inscriptions on hard surfaces like rock, pillars or metal plates are epigraphic sources.

qa.q: Which of these is an archaeological source?
qa.a: A terracotta figurine dug up at a site
qa.e: Archaeological sources are material remains such as figurines, pottery, tools and buildings found through excavation.

qa.q: Which text on administration, taxation and the duties of rulers is credited to Kautilya?
qa.e: The Arthashastra, credited to Kautilya, discusses statecraft, administration and economic management.

qa.q: Why do historians compare several sources about the same event?
qa.a: Because one source may be incomplete or show only one point of view
qa.e: A single source can be biased or incomplete. Comparing sources helps historians reach a more reliable picture.

qa.q: Which scientific method helps find the age of ancient remains such as bones, wood or charcoal?
qa.e: Carbon-14 dating measures how much radioactive carbon is left in once-living material to estimate its age.

qa.q: A record listing the births and marriages in a family over many generations is called a
qa.e: Genealogical records trace family lineage across generations.

qa.q: A king's inscription says he was the greatest ruler on earth. What should a careful historian think?
qa.a: It is useful evidence but may exaggerate, so it should be checked
qa.e: Royal inscriptions were often written to praise the ruler. They are valuable, but their claims must be compared with other evidence.

qa.q: Studying a flood using geography, economics, political science and history together is called
qa.e: Using many disciplines together to understand one problem is an interdisciplinary approach.

qa.q: What does the 'spatial perspective' in geography focus on?
qa.a: Where something is located and why that location matters
qa.e: Spatial means related to space or location. Geographers ask where things are and why.

qa.q: What does vasudhaiva kutumbakam mean?
qa.e: This ancient Sanskrit phrase expresses the idea that all people of the world are like one family.

qa.q: Which tool would a geographer use to study land use with computer maps and layers of data?
qa.e: GIS combines maps with data, for example showing rainfall, roads and villages together.

qa.q: In a drought, which question belongs to Economics?
qa.a: How did the farmers' incomes change?
qa.e: Income, prices and jobs are economic questions.

qa.q: Which is the best meaning of sustainable development?
qa.a: Meeting present needs without harming future generations' ability to meet theirs
qa.e: Sustainable development balances today's needs with the needs of people in the future.

qa.q: Panchayati Raj is often used as an example of which idea in Political Science?
qa.a: Democracy at the grassroots, with local people taking part in decisions
qa.e: Panchayati Raj lets villagers take part in local planning and decisions, which is democracy at the grassroots level.

qa.q: Why does a historian studying the growth of a town also need geography?
qa.a: Because rivers, land and climate influence where and how towns grow
qa.e: Physical features like rivers and fertile land help explain why towns grew in particular places.

qa.q: Which is the only human species living today?
qa.e: All people alive today belong to Homo sapiens. The other species died out.

qa.q: How did Palaeolithic people mainly get their food?
qa.a: By hunting animals and gathering wild plants
qa.e: Palaeolithic people were hunter-gatherers who depended directly on nature for food.

qa.q: What are microliths?
qa.a: Tiny stone tools often fitted into handles
qa.e: Microliths are small stone blades and points, typical of the Mesolithic period, often fixed into wooden or bone handles.

qa.q: The Bhimbetka rock shelters are famous mainly for
qa.e: Bhimbetka in Madhya Pradesh preserves rock paintings made by early people.

qa.q: Which early human species is linked with handaxes and cleavers and with early movement out of Africa?
qa.e: Homo erectus made handaxes and cleavers and spread from Africa into Asia and Europe.

qa.q: How did people communicate before writing was invented?
qa.a: Through speech, gestures, paintings and body decoration
qa.e: Spoken language, gestures, rock art, engravings and body decoration were ways of sharing ideas before writing.

qa.q: Why did early humans keep moving from place to place?
qa.a: To search for food and water as seasons and animals moved
qa.e: Hunter-gatherers followed animals, ripening plants and water sources, so they moved with the seasons.

qa.q: Archaeologists make copies of ancient stone tools and use them to cut meat. Why?
qa.a: To test how the tools were made and used
qa.e: Using replicas helps archaeologists understand how early people made and used their tools.

qa.q: What was the most important change of the Neolithic revolution?
qa.a: People began farming and domesticating animals
qa.e: The Neolithic revolution was the shift from hunting and gathering to farming and herding.

qa.q: Mehrgarh, one of the earliest farming villages in South Asia, is located in
qa.e: Mehrgarh lies in Balochistan, in present-day Pakistan, near the Bolan Pass.

qa.q: Which crops were grown at Mehrgarh?
qa.e: Remains of wheat and barley have been found at Mehrgarh.

qa.q: Why did farming lead to permanent villages?
qa.a: Because farmers had to stay near their fields and look after crops
qa.e: Crops take months to grow and need care, so farmers settled near their fields.

qa.q: Which type of stone tools is typical of the Neolithic period?
qa.e: Neolithic people ground and polished their stone tools, making them smoother and sharper.

qa.q: How did surplus food change society?
qa.a: Some people could become craftspeople such as potters and weavers
qa.e: When farmers produced extra food, others could be fed while they specialised in crafts.

qa.q: The Chalcolithic age is so called because people used
qa.e: Chalco means copper and lithic means stone, so it is the Copper-Stone age.

qa.q: Which was a new problem faced by settled farming communities?
qa.a: Crop failure and protecting stored grain
qa.e: Settled farmers depended on harvests, so a failed crop or stolen grain could cause hunger.

qa.q: In which present-day state of India is Dholavira located?
qa.e: Dholavira is in the Rann of Kutch in Gujarat.

qa.q: The Great Bath was found at
qa.e: The Great Bath, a large brick-lined tank, is one of the best-known structures of Mohenjo-daro.

qa.q: Which feature shows that Harappan cities were well planned?
qa.a: Streets at right angles and covered drains
qa.e: Grid-like streets, baked-brick houses and covered drains show careful town planning.

qa.q: Harappan smaller weights followed the pattern 1, 2, 4, 8, ... What is the next weight in this pattern?
qa.e: Each weight doubles the previous one, so after 8 comes 16.

qa.q: What did Mesopotamian records probably call the Harappan region?
qa.e: Mesopotamian texts mention trade with 'Meluhha', which scholars generally identify with the Harappan region.

qa.q: Why is the Harappan script still a mystery?
qa.a: Inscriptions are short and no bilingual key has been found
qa.e: Thousands of short inscriptions exist, but without a bilingual text the signs cannot be confidently read.

qa.q: Which Harappan site in Gujarat is known for its dockyard?
qa.e: Lothal had a large brick basin that many archaeologists identify as a dockyard for boats.

qa.q: The Harappan civilisation is called a Bronze Age civilisation because
qa.a: its people used bronze, an alloy of copper and tin, for tools and objects
qa.e: Harappans made tools, vessels and figures of bronze, which marks the Bronze Age.

qa.q: What does 'Mesopotamia' mean?
qa.e: Mesopotamia lay between the Tigris and Euphrates rivers, which is what its Greek name means.

qa.q: Cuneiform writing was made by
qa.a: pressing wedge-shaped marks into soft clay
qa.e: Scribes pressed a reed stylus into wet clay tablets, making wedge-shaped marks.

qa.q: Which object helped scholars decipher Egyptian hieroglyphics?
qa.e: The Rosetta Stone had the same text in hieroglyphic, Demotic and Greek; the known Greek helped decode the others.

qa.q: Why were the Nile floods important to Egyptian farmers?
qa.a: They left fertile mud on the riverbanks
qa.e: After the floods went down, rich silt was left behind, making the soil good for crops.

qa.q: What were oracle bones used for in ancient China?
qa.a: Seeking answers about the future by reading cracks
qa.e: Bones or shells were heated and the cracks were interpreted as answers to questions, a practice called divination.

qa.q: The Code of Hammurabi was a set of
qa.a: laws issued by a king of Babylon
qa.e: Hammurabi, king of Babylon in Mesopotamia, issued a written code of laws.

qa.q: Along which river did early Chinese civilisation develop?
qa.e: Early Chinese civilisation grew along the Huang He, also called the Yellow River.

qa.q: Why did Egyptians mummify the bodies of the dead?
qa.a: Because they believed in life after death
qa.e: Egyptians believed the dead continued to exist in another life, so they preserved bodies carefully.

qa.q: What was a 'janapada'?
qa.a: The land where a jana settled
qa.e: Janapada literally means the land where the jana set its foot, that is, settled.

qa.q: According to Buddhist and Jaina texts, how many mahajanapadas were there?
qa.e: These texts list sixteen mahajanapadas, including Magadha, Kosala, Vatsa and Avanti.

qa.q: Which of these were Vedic assemblies that could check the raja's power?
qa.e: The sabha and samiti (along with the vidatha) were assemblies where important matters were discussed.

qa.q: Which mahajanapada became the most powerful?
qa.e: Magadha grew strongest thanks to fertile land, rivers, iron ore and strong rulers, and later became the base of the Mauryan Empire.

qa.q: How did iron tools help the growth of settlements in the Ganga plains?
qa.a: They helped clear forests and plough more land
qa.e: Iron axes and ploughshares made it easier to clear land and grow more crops, which supported more people.

qa.q: Pataliputra, a later capital of Magadha, is the present-day city of
qa.e: Pataliputra lay where Patna in Bihar stands today.

qa.q: Northern Black Polished Ware is best described as
qa.a: glossy black pottery of the Ganga plains
qa.e: NBPW is a fine, shiny black pottery, sometimes called 'deluxe ware', found in the middle Ganga region.

qa.q: In early times, who led a jana?
qa.e: The leader of a jana was called the raja, who was advised by assemblies.

qa.q: Who founded the Mauryan Empire?
qa.e: Chandragupta Maurya, with the help of Chanakya, defeated Dhana Nanda and founded the empire.

qa.q: Which war led Ashoka to adopt the policy of Dhamma?
qa.e: After the great suffering of the Kalinga war, Ashoka turned to Dhamma and gave up wars of conquest.

qa.q: Ashoka's Dhamma mainly stressed
qa.e: Dhamma was a moral code of good conduct towards all, spread through Ashoka's edicts.

qa.q: Which three rulers have inscriptions on the Junagadh rock near Girnar?
qa.e: The rock carries records of Ashoka (Mauryan), Rudradaman I (Shaka) and Skandagupta (Gupta).

qa.q: Who composed the Prayaga inscription praising Samudragupta?
qa.e: Harishena, a court poet and official of Samudragupta, composed this praise (prashasti).

qa.q: The 'tripartite struggle' was fought for control of which city?
qa.e: The Palas, Gurjara-Pratiharas and Rashtrakutas fought over Kannauj, an important city of the Ganga plains.

qa.q: In which script were most of Ashoka's edicts written?
qa.e: Most Ashokan edicts are in Prakrit, written in the Brahmi script.

qa.q: Which kingdoms ruled the far south of India in the early centuries?
qa.e: The Cholas, Cheras and Pandyas were the three ruling families of the far south, mentioned in Sangam poems.

qa.q: What was kudavolai?
qa.a: A Chola-period way of choosing village committee members by drawing palm-leaf tickets from a pot
qa.e: Names were written on palm leaves (olai), put in a pot (kudam) and drawn out, as recorded in the Uthiramerur inscriptions.

qa.q: Who was the samaharta in ancient administration?
qa.a: The official in charge of collecting revenue
qa.e: The samaharta supervised the collection of revenue for the kingdom.

qa.q: The ideal of a 'chakravarti samrat' refers to
qa.a: a ruler whose authority extends over a vast land
qa.e: The chakravarti was an ideal of a ruler whose rule covered much of the subcontinent.

qa.q: Where are the inscriptions that describe the kudavolai system found?
qa.e: The Uthiramerur inscriptions of the Chola period describe village assemblies and kudavolai.

qa.q: Which ancient text, credited to Kautilya, discusses how a king should rule?
qa.e: The Arthashastra discusses administration, taxes, officials and the duties of rulers.

qa.q: Which ritual was performed by ancient kings to show their power?
qa.e: The ashvamedha (horse sacrifice) and the rajasuya were royal rituals that displayed a king's authority.

qa.q: Why did large kingdoms divide land into provinces, districts and villages?
qa.a: To manage taxes, law and order more easily
qa.e: Dividing territory let officials at each level handle revenue and local matters.

qa.q: Who looked after the affairs of a village in ancient kingdoms?
qa.e: The gramika was the village headman, helped by village assemblies.

qa.q: What was a shreni?
qa.a: A guild of merchants or artisans
qa.e: Shrenis were associations of traders and craftspeople that set standards and even handled deposits.

qa.q: The Nashik cave inscription records that Ushavadata deposited 2,000 kahapanas with one weavers' guild and 1,000 with another. What was the total deposit?
qa.e: 2,000 + 1,000 = 3,000 kahapanas were deposited with the guilds.

qa.q: What does the Nashik endowment show about guilds?
qa.a: Guilds also acted like banks, accepting deposits and paying interest
qa.e: The guilds held the money and paid monthly interest, which supported the monks.

qa.q: What do early Vedic texts suggest about occupations?
qa.a: They were fairly flexible; one family could have a poet, a physician and a grain grinder
qa.e: A Rig Vedic verse describes members of one family doing different kinds of work. Occupations became more hereditary later.

qa.q: Which of these were great ancient centres of learning?
qa.e: Takshashila, Nalanda and later Vikramashila attracted students from many lands.

qa.q: In a gurukula, students
qa.a: lived with their teacher and learned many subjects
qa.e: Students stayed with the guru, followed a simple disciplined life and studied subjects from grammar to medicine and astronomy.

qa.q: The Alvars and Nayanars were
qa.a: Tamil devotional saints of Vishnu and Shiva
qa.e: The Alvars sang in devotion to Vishnu and the Nayanars to Shiva, in Tamil.

qa.q: Who built the Sudarshana lake dam in Mauryan times?
qa.a: Pushyagupta, a governor of Chandragupta Maurya
qa.e: Pushyagupta, a provincial governor under Chandragupta Maurya, built the dam; Rudradaman I later repaired it.

qa.q: In which year did the Delhi Sultanate begin?
qa.e: Qutbuddin Aibak became the first Sultan of Delhi in 1206.

qa.q: Who defeated the army of Muhammad Ghuri near Mount Abu in 1178?
qa.e: Naiki Devi of the Chalukya kingdom of Gujarat, ruling on behalf of her young son, defeated Ghuri's army near Mount Abu.

qa.q: Who won the first battle of Tarain in 1191?
qa.e: Prithviraj Chauhan won the first battle in 1191; Ghuri won the second in 1192.

qa.q: What was an iqta?
qa.a: A revenue assignment given to officers in the Delhi Sultanate
qa.e: Sultans assigned the revenue of an area, an iqta, to officers who maintained soldiers and kept order there.

qa.q: The first battle of Panipat in 1526 was fought between
qa.e: Babur defeated Ibrahim Lodi, the last Sultan of Delhi, and founded Mughal rule.

qa.q: Vijayanagara was founded in 1336 by
qa.e: The brothers Harihara and Bukka founded the Vijayanagara kingdom on the banks of the Tungabhadra.

qa.q: Under Akbar, each Mughal official was given a rank called a
qa.e: The mansab fixed an official's rank, salary and the number of soldiers he had to maintain.

qa.q: How many years did the Delhi Sultanate last, from 1206 to 1526?
In which year was the battle of Haldighati fought?
qa.e: Maharana Pratap fought the Mughal army at Haldighati in 1576.

qa.q: Who supported Maharana Pratap in the Aravalli hills?
qa.e: The Bhils knew the hills and forests well and helped Maharana Pratap continue his struggle.

qa.q: What does 'Swarajya' mean?
qa.e: Swarajya means rule by one's own people, free from outside control. It was central to Shivaji's aims.

qa.q: Shivaji's council of eight ministers was called the
qa.e: Ashta means eight and pradhan means minister. The Ashtapradhan helped Shivaji run his state.

qa.q: Rana Sanga of Mewar fought Babur at the battle of
qa.e: Rana Sanga led a large alliance against Babur at Khanua in 1527.

qa.q: Which was a main reason for the Jat uprisings against the Mughals?
qa.e: The Jats were mostly farmers, and heavy taxes on their produce caused hardship and anger.

qa.q: Why were hill forts important in Maratha resistance?
qa.a: The steep terrain made them hard to attack and good bases for surprise raids
qa.e: Forts on steep hills could be defended by small forces and used as bases for quick attacks.

qa.q: Shivaji was crowned Chhatrapati in 1674. How many years after the battle of Haldighati (1576) was this?
Who founded the Ahom kingdom?
qa.e: Sukaphaa founded the Ahom kingdom in Assam in 1228.

qa.q: Under the paik system of the Ahoms,
qa.a: men served the state by turns as soldiers or workers in return for land
qa.e: Paiks worked for the state in rotation, giving the kingdom an organised army and labour force.

qa.q: The battle of Saraighat (1671) was fought
qa.e: Saraighat lies on the Brahmaputra near Guwahati, where the Ahoms defeated the Mughal fleet.

qa.q: Who led the Ahom forces at Saraighat?
qa.e: Lachit Borphukan was the Ahom commander whose leadership is remembered on Lachit Divas.

qa.q: The Ahom kingdom lasted from 1228 to 1826. For about how many years did it last?
qa.e: 1826 - 1228 = 598 years, which is nearly six hundred years.

qa.q: Which Sanskrit poem by Gangadevi describes Kumara Kampana's campaign to Madurai?
qa.e: Gangadevi, Kumara Kampana's wife, wrote Madhura Vijayam ('the conquest of Madurai').

qa.q: Krishnadevaraya wrote Amuktamalyada in which language?
qa.e: Krishnadevaraya composed Amuktamalyada in Telugu.

qa.q: What happened after the battle of Talikota in 1565?
qa.a: The Vijayanagara capital was sacked, but Nayaka rulers carried its traditions forward
qa.e: An alliance of Deccan Sultanates defeated Vijayanagara and sacked its capital; Nayaka rulers continued many of its traditions.

qa.q: Which word best means 'enduring hardship, adapting and recovering'?
qa.e: Resilience is the ability to bounce back. Resistance is opposing something.

qa.q: In which year did Guru Gobind Singh found the Khalsa?
qa.e: Guru Gobind Singh founded the Khalsa at Anandpur Sahib on Baisakhi in 1699.

qa.q: Guru Hargobind's ideas of 'miri' and 'piri' stand for
qa.e: Miri means worldly or temporal authority and piri means spiritual authority.

qa.q: Who wrote the Ramcharitmanas?
qa.e: Tulsidas wrote the Ramcharitmanas in Awadhi.

qa.q: Which saint is known for nirguna bhakti, devotion to a God without form?
qa.e: Kabir worshipped a formless God and criticised empty rituals in his dohas.

qa.q: Who built the present Kashi Vishwanath temple in 1780?
qa.e: Ahilyabai Holkar, the ruler of Indore, built the present temple in Varanasi in 1780.

qa.q: What was a hundi?
qa.a: A letter of credit used by merchants
qa.e: A hundi let a merchant deposit money in one place and collect it in another, so traders did not have to carry cash.

qa.q: A Sufi saint's centre, where disciples gathered and travellers were welcomed, was called a
qa.e: Sufi saints lived and taught in khanqahs, which were open to people of many backgrounds.
